An easy step for me in the mornings is waking up to wanting to write in my journal. Lately I’ve bounced around writing apps a bit. There are such nice journaling alternatives. What I always seem to end up with is basic Markdown files. One for each day. I even have an automation in Apple Shortcuts that creates a new one at 3am. The path to writing in the journal really is about space. Giving me space to just write without fancy plugins and themes. Probably why Markdown writers like iA Writer work well.

Writing blog posts and notes for my 11ty blog is simpler. I need a Markdown editor that respects yaml frontmatter. Some editors I might like to use fall away for various reasons. I had decided before I wanted my journals saved as local Markdown files. This has become less important since an app like diarly easily exports the files.

The “ Blinker ” EP contains 5, percussive house numbers from Canadians 22gsn and Mood Hut . The opening “ Diorama Of The World ” is busy, bustling, broken. Muted, drifting dub techno textures vying with tumbling, rattling collisions. Bass burps bumping improvised, intersecting loops. “ Spot ” is similar, but with a more rigid, 4 / 4, and a liberal sprinkling of Sci-Fi sound effects. With “ Vocal ” in parentheses, its voices are gated, fragmented and used as another percussion instrument. “ Untitled (Atmos Mix) ” is dynamite piece of Idjut Boys-esque dub house disco. items.title: Preserving 30 years of Salon journalism
items.label: Hobbies and Creative
items.excerpt:
When Salon launched in 1995, the web was still finding its voice. One of the first major publications born on the internet, Salon helped define a new kind of digital journalism, bringing together politics, culture, criticism, and ideas for a generation of online readers.

After 31 years, Salon has announced that it is ceasing publication. But thanks to web archiving, the stories don’t have to disappear.

The Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine has been preserving Salon for nearly three decades—the online publication has been published over time at salon1999.com, salonmag.com and, since 1999, salon.com. Today, more than 250,000 Salon articles can be discovered through the Wayback Machine, representing a record of digital journalism and the conversations that shaped our culture since the earliest days of the web.

To make exploring this web archive easier, we’ve also launched an experimental Salon Explorer, a new interface for discovering Salon’s archived journalism. Browse more than…

items.title: An Unattended Bug-Fixing Agent: Temporal, Jira, a Cloud VM, and a Draft Pull Request
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
For the last few weeks, I have been building a system at work that picks small bugs from Jira, gives each one to a coding agent running in a cloud development VM, and gets back a draft pull request that a developer reviews. Nobody starts the agent by hand. A Temporal schedule wakes up every ten minutes during business hours, looks at the backlog, and decides on its own which tickets are worth a try. I built most of it with an AI coding agent as my pair, which is a fun loop: an agent writing the system that runs agents.

This article walks through the full flow: how Temporal orchestrates it, how tickets are found and scored in Jira, how the VM and the agent are created, how the pull request gets opened, and how every hop is authenticated with short-lived transaction tokens instead of long-lived keys. I also cover the documentation structure we adopted for the product, because I think it is the piece that will move the productivity gain from where it is today to something much…

Some noir men stumble into trouble. Ralph Cotter gets there early, sizes up the room, and figures out who he can squeeze. In Kiss Tomorrow Goodbye (1950), James Cagney plays a criminal who treats other people’s weaknesses as opportunities to get what he wants. Fear, desire, professional respectability, and power; just about everything has a price, and Cotter wastes no time finding it. The pleasure is in watching him work; the ugliness is in how little he has to work against to get it. For the bulk of my weekdays, you can find me working at one of a handful of national gym chains. It’s one part sales, one part janitor, and one part “Sure, I’ll cancel your membership, bro. I’m not paid enough to force you to get a lawyer involved.”

The one in charge!

Really?

I had observed, just seconds ago, that spectacular nosedive.

items.label: Hobbies and Creative

I've used the mobile app on an Android phone for a week and today decided to try opening in on mobile Firefox instead. I don't see how the native mobile app improves the experience.

They are different and perhaps the sidebar implementation on the browser website is more awkward than the app's solution, but you still have the same options and you can still use all the desktop website themes. The dedicated app has a single light and dark theme that offers less contrast, especially inside topics where all the text is the same colour. How can I give up on the tasty looking Dracula theme for that?

I will give the app its dues, it has the most obvious interface for posting new topics. It took me longer to figure out desktop and mobile. Anyway, all power to Tildes and may it replace Reddit some day.

items.title: Before improving a system, decide how you’ll measure the result
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
If You Don’t Measure Something, You Can’t Improve It

You’d be surprised how often I’ve found myself in engineering discussions asking how often something occurs and getting a blank stare.

Without any measurement, you are operating on vibes alone.

Engineering teams are always looking to improve something: maybe you want to reduce latency, increase system throughput, reduce production incidents, or make a dent in your pull request queue.
Yet time and time again, I see teams start changing systems without any way to measure the results.
Something might feel faster, or incidents might feel less frequent; but are they?

Before I improve anything, I make sure I can measure it.

Measure to Understand

The first step to improving anything is understanding where you are today.

Take latency as an example.
If you want to improve a system's end-to-end response time, start by measuring it.

How long does a single request take?
What’s the average?
The 90th percentile?

items.title: What Cooperation Does Not Concede
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
One of you glances toward an open window and says, “It’s getting cold in here.” Your housemate closes it. Both know what was wanted. Neither has had to announce who is entitled to give the other instructions.

An indirect request can separate agreement to an action from agreement about who may demand it. The literal remark supplies a description both can accept: one person mentioned a problem; the other chose to help. If the window stays open, the remark can be allowed to pass without anyone announcing a refusal. The intention need not be secret for the relationship to remain unspecified.

Direct requests can preserve equality. This advantage of indirection arises when an explicit request risks becoming a test of rank—and when both parties are willing to leave that test unspoken.

In August I wrote about how I built Travel Log, a private travel journal for iPhone that builds your travel history by itself. That post ended with two promises, more or less. The first was that I might publish smaller parts of the code at some point. The second was that the App Store release would come “in a few days/weeks.”

The few days/weeks turned into three months. And instead of publishing smaller parts, I published the whole thing.

As of today, Travel Log is on the App Store and its source code is on GitHub under the MIT license.

This comes down to trust. Travel Log keeps a detailed record of where you have been. The entire pitch of the app is that this record stays on your phone: no account, no server of my own, no analytics. Until now, you had to take my word for it.

items.title: Feed the Scorchpot [$14.99] [Strategy] [Windows] [macOS]
items.label: Gaming
items.excerpt:
You struck a deal with a dragon: twenty years of protection for twenty years of dinner service. The island thrives under the beast's watchful eye, as long as the meals keep coming.

Every year, the dragon wakes up hungrier. You roll dice to work your island, harvest ingredients, fuse them into recipes, and cook them down in the Scorchpot — the pot you keep full or end up in. Get the meal right and you prosper. Get it wrong and you're smoke.

Build farmsteads, shrines, and harbors across your hex-grid island, each one changing how the board pays out. The best runs start with a handful of tiles and end with a machine that buries the dragon in food. Then the odds tighten, the dragon turns picky, and you tear the whole thing down and rebuild while it's on fire.

Feed the Scorchpot, keep the dragon happy, and outlast the contract.

Cook cleverly, plan badly, or just roll with it — the dragon doesn't care how you win, only that you feed the beast on time. And yes, you can pet the…

items.title: Juice Galaxy (formerly Juice World) [$5.00] [Role Playing] [Windows] [macOS] [Linux]
items.label: Gaming
items.excerpt:
Juice is everything. There is nothing in the Fog. There is no greater honor than to serve the Juice Queen, and the sky is definitely not made of plywood.

Juice Galaxy is a happy place to fly around and smack things and drink juice. And explore things. And just, flip around doing stuff. Use any of a multitude of weapons to clobber and devour the local wildlife. Gather juice to increase your power and take on more powerful enemies.The game is still in active development. There's still a ton of work to do. I want to polish the physics and add a ton more abilities, places, music, items, monsters, and story.Enjoy, and please feel free to leave feedback or suggestions.

YouTube:https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCc7nwUzdbTKurTjjyf73U_g

items.title: Keepsake County [$24.99] [Shooter] [Windows] [macOS] [Linux]
items.label: Gaming
items.excerpt:
Burglarize hideous farmhouses in the middle of nowhere and get outta dodge.

You have moments before the cops arrive to rob a procedurally-generated house that you've never seen before. If you're caught, residents will call the police even sooner... or take the law into their own hands.

Never played an extraction shooter or an immersive sim before? This game is for you, designed for people interested in those genres, but scared to dip their toes in!

Keepsake County walks a delicate tightrope act between traditional Immersive Sim, Extraction Shooter, and Roguelite, while swapping through the guises of exaggerated 90s cartoon comedy and satirical, melancholic americana.

You are Samuel “Sammie” Sack, a fresh-faced (and very short), 19-year-old thief whose father just got sent to jail for armed robbery, in the fictional state of Frikota.

Move out of your house that just got foreclosed on, learn to rob and steal, and start your quest to pay off a massive debt while trying to buy back…
